sectionCatalog: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

sections.label: About me
paragraphs: I’m Nick, a high school engineering student focused on mechanical design, robotics, mechatronics, and physical product development. I’m most interested in problems where geometry, motion, packaging, manufacturing, electronics, and user experience all have to work together.

I started designing mechanisms long before I had access to CAD or a 3D printer, experimenting with LEGO Transformers, puzzle boxes, and hand-built projects. As my tools improved, those same interests grew into fully original transforming figures, competition robots, custom electronics, mechanical puzzles, and products designed for real users.

I’m also a member of FIRST Tech Challenge Team 23268 Ultraviolet, a three-person robotics team where I work across CAD, fabrication, assembly, programming, prototyping, and testing. Working on competition robots has taught me that a design is never finished just because it works in CAD; it has to survive manufacturing, real hardware, unpredictable conditions, and the people using it.

Outside engineering, I’m a varsity swimmer and musician, playing saxophone and piano. I also spend a lot of time strength training, something I took up on my own simply because I wanted to become stronger and see how far I could push myself.

sections.label: How I design
paragraphs: I tend to obsess over making every part earn its place. I like compact mechanisms, clean packaging, serviceable systems, and designs where the complexity is hidden well enough that the final result feels obvious.

My process usually involves a lot of iteration: build something, find what I overlooked, understand why it failed, and redesign it until the solution becomes simpler and more intentional. I care about making things work, but I also care about making them understandable, durable, and worth looking at twice.

sections.label: Areas I'm interested in
paragraphs: Mechanical design · Robotics · Mechatronics · Product design · Mechanism design · CAD & surface modeling · Rapid prototyping · PCB design · Computer vision

sections.label: What I'm working toward
paragraphs: I don’t know exactly what form my work will take in the future, but I want to keep taking harder physical problems and turning them into systems that are useful, deliberate, and elegantly engineered.

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: Modular Chassis MK2 is the second generation of a drivetrain architecture I originally developed for FIRST Tech Challenge robotics. It is built around four independently removable mecanum wheel modules, each treated as a self-contained mechatronic system.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted to push the modularity of my original chassis beyond simple mechanical removal by designing the drivetrain, electrical connections, sensing, diagnostics, and cable management around serviceability from the beginning.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I am designing the complete chassis architecture and its supporting subsystems, including the removable wheel modules, gearbox and wheel cartridges, module interfaces, sensor integration, cable management, and custom electronics.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The central challenge is fitting all of these systems into an FTC-scale robot without allowing modularity or serviceability to consume excessive space or compromise structural and drivetrain performance.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: MK2 has pushed me to think less about individual parts and more about the dependencies between systems. Mechanical packaging, electronics, wiring, sensing, and maintenance all have to be designed together.

overview.label: What Changed
overview.text: MK2 began as a refinement of my previous modular chassis, but it has become a broader study of serviceable system design. Instead of asking only whether a component fits or functions, I now ask how it is installed, how it is removed, where its wiring goes, how the system identifies it, and how someone would diagnose it when something eventually fails.

overview.label: What I am Taking Forward
overview.text: The most interesting part of MK2 has become designing the dependencies between disciplines. Mechanical packaging affects sensor placement; sensors affect PCB layout; PCB geometry affects connectors; connectors affect module removal. Treating those relationships as part of the design rather than as problems to solve afterward has changed how I approach complex systems.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK2 Modular Chassis: Removable Wheel Module Architecture

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: Each corner of MK2 is an independent drivetrain module containing the wheel, motor, drivetrain, structural interfaces, wiring, and supporting electronics.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: The modules are intended to let major drivetrain components be serviced or replaced without requiring the rest of the robot to be disassembled.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I developed the module geometry, chassis interfaces, component packaging, wheel clearance, drivetrain alignment, cable routing, and service access around removal as a fundamental requirement.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: FTC robots leave very little unused volume, so features that would normally exist as separate systems have to occupy the same small envelope without interfering with one another.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Serviceability works best when it determines the architecture from the beginning rather than being added after the major mechanical decisions have already been made.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK2 Modular Chassis: Wheel Cartridge Development

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: The wheel-side cartridge allows the wheel and associated drivetrain components to be separated from the larger module as another removable subsystem.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted wheel-side components to be independently serviceable and replaceable without removing or rebuilding the entire drivetrain module.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I developed the cartridge, axle support, bearing arrangement, wheel retention, bevel-drive geometry, and its interface with the surrounding module.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: An early design met the functional requirements but increased the module width by approximately 5 mm. I redesigned the system around a two-part axle and coupler arrangement to recover much of that space while preserving the cartridge concept.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Modularity has its own packaging cost. A removable subsystem is only useful if the interfaces needed to create it do not compromise the performance or size of the larger machine.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK2 Modular Chassis: Gearbox Cassette & Automatic Identification

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: The drivetrain is being developed around a removable gearbox cassette that isolates the bevel-drive components as another serviceable assembly.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: Separating the gearbox from the surrounding structure makes drivetrain servicing easier and creates the possibility of changing configurations without redesigning the entire wheel module.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the cassette architecture and am integrating an identification system using a magnet and Hall-effect sensor so the module can detect what removable component is installed.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The available space forced the sensing hardware to become part of the gearbox architecture itself. Sensor orientation, magnet distance, drivetrain geometry, and service access all compete for the same volume.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Mechatronic features work best when the mechanical and electrical requirements are developed together rather than when sensors are added after the mechanism is finished.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK2 Modular Chassis: Custom Module Management PCB

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: The module management PCB is a custom circuit board that consolidates the sensors and electrical interfaces inside each wheel module.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: As MK2 gained more sensors and removable components, point-to-point wiring began working against the modularity of the mechanical system. A dedicated PCB provides a cleaner and more repeatable electrical interface.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the board in KiCad, including the component layout, connectors, copper routing, power distribution, signal connections, and physical dimensions. Rev A used an eight-pin output interface; Rev B added motor-encoder support and expanded the bus to ten pins.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The board has to fit within an approximately 24.5 × 35.5 mm envelope while maintaining connector access and practical routing. I moved from a front-layer-heavy first layout to a cleaner two-layer design as the circuit became more complex.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: PCB design is also mechanical design. Connector placement, cable direction, board mounting, service access, and available volume affect the circuit just as much as the schematic does.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK2 Modular Chassis: Sensor & Diagnostic Integration

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: MK2 incorporates sensors for motor feedback, temperature, vibration, and removable-component identification.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I want each drivetrain module to provide useful information about its own configuration and condition rather than functioning as a completely passive mechanical assembly.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: The current architecture includes motor encoder feedback, thermistors, Hall-effect identification, and an ADXL345 accelerometer. I have also developed mounting and enclosure concepts that integrate these devices into the module.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: Collecting data is easy compared with collecting useful data. Sensors have to be positioned and mounted so their measurements actually represent the condition I am trying to observe without interfering with the rest of the module.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: More sensing does not automatically create a better system. I have been evaluating each sensor around whether its information could meaningfully improve inspection, maintenance, or troubleshooting.

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: IDW Ratchet MK2 is a complete redesign of my original transforming Ratchet figure, again based on his appearance in the 2005 IDW comic Infiltration. It converts between the character’s robot form and van mode while aiming to reproduce the comic geometry as closely as possible.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: MK1 proved that the character could be turned into a functional transforming figure, but both modes were noticeably compromised by blocky proportions and geometry designed around the transformation rather than the source material. For MK2, I reversed that priority: I established the comic-accurate forms first and am designing the transformation around them with as little visual compromise as possible.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I am designing the complete figure from scratch, including both modes, transformation sequence, articulation, panel movement, internal packaging, joint architecture, and printable component breakdown. The design uses comic panels as the primary reference rather than an existing toy, since this version of Ratchet has never received an official transforming figure.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The comic design leaves almost no convenient space for transformation. Large vehicle panels are already visually assigned to specific parts of the robot, while the remaining van geometry still has to disappear somewhere inside a relatively thin humanoid form. This sharply limits where components can move and forces mechanisms to share extremely small volumes without altering the exterior proportions.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: MK2 has pushed me to treat visual accuracy itself as an engineering constraint rather than something adjusted after the mechanism works. Instead of simplifying difficult geometry, I have had to develop better transformations, more controlled surface modeling, and tighter packaging to preserve it.

overview.label: Comic Accuracy & Transformation Packaging
overview.text: The main goal of MK2 is to make both modes look intentional even when compared directly with the comic. Major body panels, leg proportions, vehicle surfaces, and silhouette are being matched to the artwork before their transformation paths are finalized. This makes the transformation significantly harder than MK1. Many of the large panels that could otherwise be moved wherever convenient are visually locked to specific robot body parts by the source material. The rest of the vehicle then has to fold around those fixed relationships. So far, the compromises have remained small. One example is the heel geometry, which extends slightly farther backward than the comic model to provide the required transformation clearance and also improves standing stability. I have tried to treat compromises like this as controlled engineering decisions rather than allowing them to accumulate across the design.

overview.label: Surface Modeling & CAD Reconstruction
overview.text: Achieving the comic’s smooth, rounded forms has also required a different CAD workflow from the more geometric MK1 design. Some organic components were initially shaped in Blender and brought into Fusion 360, but mesh-based geometry created visible faceting and was not ideal for a model intended to become a manufacturable mechanical assembly. For areas such as the knee armor, I rebuilt the geometry using controlled patches and lofted surfaces in Fusion rather than relying on the original mesh. This required substantially more work but produced smooth, editable surfaces that integrate cleanly with joints and surrounding components. The project has therefore become as much an exercise in surface quality and manufacturable form development as it is in transformation design.

overview.label: Current Development
overview.text: Both the robot and vehicle geometry are being developed together so that changes in one mode can be evaluated immediately against the other. The van mode has become especially useful for exposing packaging problems because its large, continuous exterior surfaces leave very little room to hide dimensional errors. The current model is still being refined with additional joints, clearances, edge treatment, and surface details before physical prototyping. The overall proportions and major transformation architecture are already established, allowing later work to focus on making the mechanisms printable, durable, and repeatable without sacrificing the comic-accurate exterior.

projects.title: Sea of Thieves "An Introduction to the Gold Hoarders" Puzzle Box

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: A physical puzzle box that recreates the full Gold Hoarders tutorial voyage from Sea of Thieves. Instead of simply borrowing the game’s visual style, each major action from the voyage is translated into a physical puzzle, mechanism, or interaction.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted to explore whether a digital gameplay sequence could be converted into a completely physical experience while preserving the same sense of progression. The goal is for someone familiar with the game to recognize what they are doing at every stage, while still allowing the box to function as a standalone mechanical puzzle.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I am designing the complete puzzle sequence, mechanical interlocks, compass-navigation system, sliding map puzzle, miniature Sailor’s Chest, Gold Hoarders tent interaction, dialogue-release mechanisms, reward drawer, and progression token. Each stage unlocks or reveals the next, preventing the solver from accessing later parts of the voyage before completing the required earlier actions.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The largest challenge is translating actions that are effortless in a video game like sailing, navigating, digging up treasure, returning to an outpost, and selling loot, into physical mechanisms that communicate the same meaning without relying on a screen. The box also has to mechanically verify solutions and control the order of progression without making the experience feel overly guided.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project has pushed me beyond designing individual puzzles and toward designing an entire sequence of interactions. Mechanical logic, narrative pacing, user interpretation, and physical feedback all have to reinforce one another so the solver understands not only what changed, but what that change represents within the voyage.

overview.label: Voyage to Mechanism Progression
overview.text: The puzzle begins locked and requires a tool earned from a previous puzzle box to start the voyage. Using that tool releases the first narrative sheet, with a treasure map printed on its reverse side. The solver compares the map’s destination coordinates with a marked starting location on the exterior of the box, determines the required direction of travel, and sets a physical compass dial accordingly. The correct heading unlocks the lid, representing sailing to the island and revealing the next stage of the puzzle. Later, the same navigation system is reused in reverse. After recovering the treasure, the solver must determine the opposite heading to represent sailing back to the starting outpost. This allows one mechanism to carry different meaning depending on where the solver is in the overall sequence.

overview.label: Self-Verifying Sliding Map Puzzle
overview.text: Opening the lid reveals a sliding-tile puzzle representing the island treasure map. The goal is to reconstruct the map and locate the marked treasure position. Rather than checking the solution with a single exposed button or hole, the center tile is spring-loaded and mechanically blocked by the surrounding pieces. Clearance features beneath the tiles only align when the entire puzzle is arranged correctly. Once every surrounding tile reaches its intended position, the center tile can rise automatically. This movement represents digging up the treasure while simultaneously verifying the solution mechanically and releasing the compartment containing the miniature Sailor’s Chest.

overview.label: Physical Storytelling & Dialogue System
overview.text: The voyage includes narrative instructions and reactions throughout the experience. I am preserving those moments through physical dialogue sheets released at specific points in the puzzle. Instead of presenting all instructions at the beginning, individual sheets emerge only when the corresponding mechanical action has been completed. This allows the dialogue to act as both story content and controlled guidance while keeping later stages hidden until they become relevant. The paper-release mechanisms also make progression visible in a different way from drawers and moving parts: completing an action does not merely unlock another mechanism; it advances the story.

overview.label: Selling the Treasure & Final Reward
overview.text: Recovering the miniature Sailor’s Chest does not complete the puzzle. Just as in Sea of Thieves, the treasure still has to be returned and sold. After navigating back to the outpost, a previously hidden exterior panel becomes removable, revealing the distinctive green canvas of the Gold Hoarders tent and a chest-shaped receiving slot. The solver must recognize that the physical chest recovered earlier is now another functional puzzle component. A hidden magnetic element inside the chest activates the mechanism behind the tent when inserted correctly, releasing the final reward drawer. Inside is a silver Gold Hoarders voyage coin representing completion of the tutorial. The opposite face carries the symbol of the next voyage, with raised geometry that physically functions as the key required to begin the next puzzle box.

overview.label: Connected Puzzle Series
overview.text: This box is designed as one part of a larger physical progression based on Sea of Thieves. The tool required to start this puzzle is earned by completing the preceding Maiden Voyage box, while the coin earned at the end becomes the input required for the next Gold Hoarders voyage. The result is a chain in which rewards are not only collectibles but functional components of later puzzles. Completing one experience physically changes what the solver is capable of accessing next.

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: Modular Chassis MK1 is an FTC drivetrain chassis built around four independently removable mecanum wheel modules. Each corner contains its own motor, wheel, drivetrain components, wiring, and structural interface with the central robot.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted routine drivetrain maintenance to require less disassembly. Instead of building motors, wheels, and wiring permanently into the robot frame, I designed each corner so the entire drivetrain assembly could be removed as a unit.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the complete chassis architecture, including all four wheel modules, their structural mounting system, guide geometry, retention hardware, drivetrain packaging, and a dedicated mechanism for managing the module wiring during removal.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The largest challenge was making a module removable without creating new problems in alignment, structural stiffness, drivetrain packaging, or wiring. Every interface had to locate the module consistently while still allowing it to come out without dismantling surrounding parts of the robot.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project taught me that modularity is primarily an interface problem. Separating a machine into pieces is easy; making those pieces reconnect mechanically and electrically in a predictable way requires much more deliberate design.

overview.label: Accolades
overview.text: This chassis won a 'You Inspire Me' pin from a judge at the 2026 FTC World Championship. Each judge has only one such pin to give, making it very rare.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK1 Modular Chassis: Removable Wheel Modules

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: The chassis uses four self-contained mecanum drivetrain modules, one at each corner of the robot. Each module packages a goBILDA motor, drivetrain, wheel, wiring, and the structure needed to transfer loads into the main chassis.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: Wheel and drivetrain problems are common points of maintenance on an FTC robot. Packaging them into removable corner assemblies made it possible to access or replace a large portion of the drivetrain without taking apart the central robot.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the module housing and drivetrain layout around a compact bevel-drive arrangement using 435 RPM goBILDA motors. The wheel, motor, gearing, structural shell, mounting features, and wiring all had to fit within one removable assembly.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The module had to remain compact while handling drivetrain loads and preserving the wheel geometry required for mecanum drive. The removable architecture also meant the module could not rely on permanent fasteners or surrounding robot structure for every constraint.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Designing a removable assembly forced me to think about a part not only in its installed state, but also about the path it takes during installation, removal, and maintenance.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: MK1 Modular Chassis: Flip-Out Wire Spool

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: Each module incorporates a small wire-management spool with a flip-out handle that controls the extra cable needed for module removal.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: Mechanical modularity would have been much less useful if removing a wheel module still required disconnecting or untangling wiring buried inside the robot. The spool gave the cable a defined place to go in both the installed and removed states.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the spool directly into the module rather than treating the wiring as an external afterthought. The handle flips outward when needed so the stored wire can be released or managed, then folds back into the module when the mechanism is not in use.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The mechanism had to store useful cable length without taking up much volume or interfering with the drivetrain. It also had to remain accessible after the rest of the module was assembled.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: The spool changed how I thought about wiring in mechanical design. A cable is still a moving physical component with bend radius, slack, routing, and service requirements, and those constraints deserve the same attention as gears or structural parts.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: IDW Ratchet MK1 is my first complete original transforming-figure design, based on Ratchet’s appearance in the 2005 IDW comic Infiltration. The design converts between a fully articulated robot and vehicle mode through an approximately 40-step transformation.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I had wanted to design a full Transformer since I first became interested in how transforming toys package one form inside another. I chose this version of Ratchet because, to my knowledge, it had never been adapted into a transforming figure, leaving me with no existing toy or transformation scheme to reverse engineer.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I developed the complete figure from the ground up, including the transformation sequence, joint architecture, robot articulation, vehicle packaging, panel movement, internal clearances, and printable part breakdown. Comic panels were my primary reference, so I had to interpret a two-dimensional character design as two compatible three-dimensional forms.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The central challenge was making two recognizable shapes occupy the same physical volume. Every robot component had to become part of the vehicle or fit somewhere inside it, while every transformation joint needed enough clearance to move without sacrificing articulation or appearance. Some areas required repeated redesigns; one shoulder mechanism alone went through eleven versions before the geometry worked.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Ratchet taught me that solving a mechanism is only one part of designing a transforming object. Sequence, tolerances, structural strength, articulation, part interference, and the user’s ability to understand the transformation all have to work together. It was the project that turned my interest in transformation mechanisms into a complete mechanical design process.

overview.label: Transformation Architecture
overview.text: Because there was no existing figure to study, every transformation movement began as an interpretation of the comic design. I worked backward and forward between robot and vehicle modes, deciding which surfaces could realistically correspond and then developing hinges, pivots, and nested assemblies to move them between positions. The finished sequence contains roughly forty steps. Many movements depend on a specific order because one component must clear another before the surrounding geometry can close. Designing that sequence became almost as important as designing the individual mechanisms themselves.

overview.label: Character Fidelity and Articulation
overview.text: I wanted the transformation to serve the character design rather than forcing either mode to look like a compromise. I used comic artwork to establish proportions, panel shapes, and recognizable visual features, then worked within those constraints to create the hidden geometry necessary for transformation. The robot was also designed as an articulated figure rather than a static transformation exercise. This meant transformation joints had to coexist with poseable shoulders, hips, knees, and other articulation without weakening the structure or consuming space needed by the alternate mode.

overview.label: Iteration and Physical Design
overview.text: Ratchet took approximately a year to develop, with many mechanisms being rebuilt as later parts of the transformation exposed problems in earlier decisions. A solution could work by itself and still fail once surrounding panels, articulation, or the full transformation sequence were added. That iterative process changed how I approach complex CAD assemblies. Instead of treating individual mechanisms as finished once they move correctly, I learned to evaluate them as parts of a larger sequence where clearance, durability, assembly, and neighboring components can all force another redesign.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: A custom machine-learning vision system developed for Tuzik, our FTC Into the Deep competition robot. The goal was to recognize game pieces across the field and provide the robot with enough information to support automated sample selection and pickup.

overview.label: Why I worked on it
overview.text: The game placed samples in varying positions, colors, orientations, distances, and lighting conditions. I wanted the robot to identify useful targets automatically rather than relying entirely on the driver to locate and align with them.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I created the training-data process, generated roughly 200,000 labeled images from videos I recorded, adapted an existing GitHub labeling project to avoid the cost of commercial labeling, configured and trained the TensorFlow model, and iterated through multiple failed setups until the model performed reliably under controlled testing.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The hardest part was discovering that a successful model did not necessarily produce a successful robotic system. After months of training and iteration, the model worked well at close range, but camera resolution limited reliable recognition at the distances the robot actually needed. Competition lighting also differed significantly from our normal testing environment, revealing another source of performance variation that was difficult to reproduce beforehand.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project changed how I think about validating engineering systems. A model can perform well under the assumptions built into its dataset and still fail when hardware or environmental conditions change. I learned to test not only whether a solution works, but also which conditions allow it to work and whether those conditions match the real problem.

overview.label: Dataset Development
overview.text: I built the training dataset from videos of FTC game pieces, using a planned matrix of variations such as distance, angle, position, lighting, and background. Rather than collecting images randomly, I changed one variable at a time so the dataset would deliberately represent the conditions I expected the robot to encounter. The resulting videos were processed into approximately 200,000 images. Because labeling that volume commercially would have been impractical, I adapted an existing open-source labeling tool so the dataset could be prepared automatically.

overview.label: Model Training & Iteration
overview.text: The first training attempts did not converge or recognize objects as expected because of mistakes in the model setup and training configuration. I repeatedly modified the pipeline, retrained the model, and compared the results until the detector became reliable. Later dataset revisions added significantly more variation, especially examples containing multiple nearby objects, because earlier versions could recognize isolated samples but struggled when several appeared close together.

overview.label: Real-World Validation
overview.text: The final model could identify samples reliably under the conditions represented in its training data, but testing exposed limitations outside the model itself. The camera's resolution prevented dependable detection at longer field distances, making the system less useful than expected for competition. At the World Championship, unusually dark field conditions and angled spotlights also demonstrated how drastically environmental changes could affect vision systems. The model was ultimately not used on the final competition robot, but the project became one of my most valuable lessons in the difference between making an algorithm work and making an entire engineered system robust.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot

projects.title: Sharik - FTC Decode Competition Robot
projects.role: Ultraviolet is a three-person team, so responsibilities are highly distributed. For this project, I was responsible for prototype design, mechanical design, manufacturing and assembly, and programming support.

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: Sharik was Team 23268 Ultraviolet’s competition robot for the FTC DECODE season. The robot used a compact mecanum drivetrain, full-width intake and transfer system, rotating turret, adjustable shooter hood, vision-assisted targeting, and autonomous routines designed around rapid artifact collection and scoring.

overview.label: Why I worked on it
overview.text: This was my second season on Ultraviolet and gave me a much larger mechanical role than the previous year. Although I was not the robot’s primary overall designer, I became one of the main prototype designers and contributed directly to final subsystem development, fabrication, assembly, testing, and redesign.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed and tested early mechanical concepts across the robot, created CAD and manufactured parts for multiple subsystems, and heavily contributed to assembly and iterative testing. My largest final design contribution was the V3 turret and shooter architecture, which I designed myself after working extensively on the earlier versions. I also provided limited programming support, primarily during development and testing of the autonomous routines.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The largest challenge was knowing when to stop refining an ambitious concept and change direction. An early robot architecture used a revolver-style cylinder I designed to sort artifacts, along with a mechanically linked firing system intended to reduce independent failure points. The system worked conceptually, but it was too slow, lacked sufficient firing power, and was consuming too much development time. We ultimately abandoned that architecture and rebuilt around a faster intake, transfer, and turreted shooter system. That pivot required giving up substantial completed work in favor of a simpler architecture that better matched competition demands.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Sharik taught me that iteration is not always about improving the current version. Sometimes the best engineering decision is recognizing that the architecture itself is wrong. I also became much more comfortable contributing to subsystem-level design, rapidly prototyping alternatives, manufacturing parts through several processes, and using repeated testing to drive mechanical decisions.

overview.label: Turret & Shooter Development
overview.text: I worked extensively on the turret throughout its development and designed the final V3 assembly myself. Earlier versions improved power transmission and packaging, but the projectile still carried unwanted backspin that reduced shot consistency. V3 added counter-rotating rollers to better control the ball as it exited the shooter, reducing backspin and improving accuracy. I also repackaged the assembly into a more compact and polished structure while integrating the flywheel, adjustable hood, guides, and Limelight vision hardware. The final system could rotate 360 degrees independently of the chassis, allowing the robot to aim without physically turning. Combined with an adjustable hood and vision-assisted targeting, this gave the robot much more control over shot direction and range.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
overview.text: A major early prototype used a revolver-style cylinder to organize and feed artifacts into a mechanically synchronized firing system. I designed the cylinder and helped develop the surrounding architecture with the goal of creating controlled, reliable indexing without relying on several separately timed mechanisms. Testing revealed that the concept was too slow for the scoring pace we needed, could not produce enough firing power, and would require too much additional development to become competitive. Rather than continue investing time into it, we pivoted to the final architecture based on a wide roller intake, fast transfer ramp, and turreted shooter. That redesign became one of the most important lessons of the season: a clever mechanism is not automatically the right mechanism if its complexity works against the larger strategic goal.

overview.label: Manufacturing, Assembly & Testing
overview.text: Because Ultraviolet remained a three-person team, I worked across nearly every stage of bringing the robot from CAD to competition hardware. I produced FDM-printed components, helped fabricate laser-cut polycarbonate and waterjet-cut aluminum parts, assembled mechanisms, and repeatedly tested revisions as the robot evolved. Much of my contribution came through this iteration loop rather than ownership of complete subsystems. I helped identify mechanical failures, adjust CAD, rebuild assemblies, and validate whether changes actually improved performance. The completed robot ultimately ranked 119th worldwide, placing it within approximately the top 2% of FTC teams.

overview.label: Accolades
overview.text: The completed robot ultimately ranked 119th worldwide, placing it within approximately the top 2% of FTC teams.

projects.title: Tuzik - FTC Into the Deep Competition Robot
projects.role: Ultraviolet is a three-person team, so responsibilities are highly distributed. For this project, I was responsible for CAD support, manufacturing, assembly, and programming.

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: Tuzik was Team 23268 Ultraviolet’s competition robot for the FTC Into the Deep season. The robot combined a compact mecanum drivetrain with horizontal intake extension, a five-stage vertical lift, separate intake and deposit claws, and a pass-through scoring system capable of handling both samples and specimens.

overview.label: Why I worked on it
overview.text: This was my first season on Ultraviolet and my first opportunity to contribute to a highly integrated competition robot on a three-person team. Although I was not the robot’s primary mechanical designer, the small team meant I was involved throughout CAD support, manufacturing, assembly, programming, testing, and competition development.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: My mechanical work focused on supporting CAD and creating smaller components such as sensor mounts, brackets, and other 3D-printed parts. I manufactured printed components, assisted with robot assembly, and participated heavily in testing and debugging. On the programming side, I assisted across opmodes and subsystems and took a larger role in vision development. I developed computer-vision logic that helped the robot detect game objects, evaluate their position and orientation, and guide the intake toward them. I also developed a much larger AI-based vision system during the season, which I document separately as its own project.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The biggest challenge I personally worked on was making vision useful to a physical robot rather than simply detecting an object on a screen. The system had to distinguish game pieces, determine which target was most useful, estimate its position and angle, and translate that information into movement of the intake and robot. Lighting, reflections, camera placement, and imperfect object orientations all affected performance.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: Tuzik taught me how different contributing to a competition robot is from designing an isolated project. A part or program is only useful if it integrates reliably with everything around it. I became more comfortable working inside another designer’s architecture, debugging systems I had not created myself, manufacturing parts for rapid iteration, and using testing feedback to improve the robot rather than treating my own work as an independent subsystem.

overview.label: Robot Architecture
overview.text: Tuzik used a compact mecanum drivetrain with belt-driven wheels and centrally packaged motors. A powered horizontal extension carried a rotating intake claw capable of approaching samples from different orientations. Collected game pieces could be transferred into a separate deposit mechanism mounted on a five-stage vertical lift. The deposit could slide horizontally through the robot, allowing samples and specimens to pass from one side of the machine to the other and reducing the need to rotate the entire chassis during scoring. The robot went through repeated subsystem revisions throughout the season as testing exposed problems with speed, stability, alignment, and reliability.

overview.label: Programming and Vision
overview.text: My largest technical contribution was computer vision. In addition to general programming support across the robot, I developed an OpenCV-based system using a separate intake camera to identify game pieces by color, evaluate their visible geometry, and determine their orientation. The resulting position and angle information could be used to align the intake and guide the robot toward an object rather than relying entirely on manual driver positioning. This required treating vision as part of the robot’s control system rather than as an isolated detection demo. I also developed a separate machine-learning vision project during this season involving a large custom training dataset and TensorFlow model. Because that project involved its own months-long development process, failures, and testing, it is documented separately in the portfolio.

overview.label: Testing, Manufacturing, and Competition
overview.text: Because Ultraviolet had only three members, testing often crossed normal role boundaries. I helped manufacture and assemble parts, test subsystem changes, identify mechanical and software bugs, and make smaller CAD revisions as issues appeared. That process gave me experience contributing effectively even when I was not leading the overall mechanical design. I learned to understand an existing system quickly, find where I could add value, and work through problems collaboratively rather than needing ownership of the complete design.

overview.label: Accolades
overview.text: The completed robot ultimately ranked 4th worldwide out of over 8,000 teams.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: The Mic is a microphone-shaped, seven-step mechanical puzzle box designed for my seven-year-old sister. Completing the sequence releases a miniature golden microphone hidden inside the puzzle.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted to create a puzzle specifically around the person solving it rather than simply designing a mechanism and choosing a recipient afterward. Because my sister was seven, I intentionally kept the sequence approachable while still giving her several distinct discoveries to work through.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the microphone-shaped enclosure, complete seven-step puzzle sequence, internal reward mechanism, miniature golden microphone, modular display stand, and custom packaging. The stand uses dovetail connections so rewards from different puzzle boxes can eventually be displayed together as a collection.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The puzzle had to balance difficulty, durability, and clarity for a young user. Each step needed to reveal enough information to suggest what might happen next without making the solution immediately obvious, while all of the mechanisms still had to fit inside a recognizable microphone form.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project changed how I thought about puzzle design. The mechanism itself was only part of the experience; difficulty, reward, presentation, and the person interacting with it all mattered. Designing around a specific user produced a better result than treating usability as something to consider after the mechanism was finished.

overview.label: Seven-step puzzle sequence
overview.text: The puzzle is solved through a sequence of seven mechanical actions distributed throughout the microphone body. I intentionally designed it as an easier puzzle so my sister could make steady progress without the experience becoming frustrating. Completing the final step releases the miniature golden microphone stored inside. The exterior was also designed to read immediately as a microphone rather than as a conventional box with mechanisms attached to it, which meant packaging the puzzle sequence within the recognizable rounded head and narrow handle.

overview.label: Packaging and presentation
overview.text: I also designed custom packaging and an internal clamshell around the puzzle. My goal was for receiving and opening The Mic to feel like receiving a finished product rather than being handed a 3D-printed mechanism. Designing the packaging alongside the puzzle made presentation part of the project itself. The enclosure, reward, stand, and packaging were all intended to contribute to the same experience before, during, and after solving it.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: The Keys is a piano-shaped mechanical puzzle box designed for my mom. It uses a nine-step solution sequence and belongs to the same puzzle-box series as The Mic, with a more difficult progression and the same reward-and-display system.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted each puzzle in the series to be tailored to its intended recipient rather than simply reusing the same mechanism in a different shell. For my mom, that meant increasing the difficulty and creating a puzzle whose form and identity fit the recipient while still belonging to the same overall product family.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the piano-shaped enclosure, nine-step puzzle sequence, internal reward mechanism, and the matching packaging presentation. The packaging uses the same overall dimensions as the other puzzle boxes in the series, but with a piano silhouette on top instead of the microphone logo. The reward system is also shared across the series, allowing the final reward to connect to the same modular display-stand system.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was increasing the difficulty without losing clarity or making the puzzle feel unfair. The mechanism had to fit inside a recognizable piano form while giving the recipient a more involved experience than the easier microphone puzzle.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project taught me more about designing a product family instead of a single object. The puzzle, reward, and packaging all had to stay consistent across the series, while the puzzle logic, external form, and difficulty level changed to suit a different user.

overview.label: Nine-Step puzzle sequence
overview.text: The Keys uses a nine-step sequence, making it more difficult than the seven-step microphone puzzle. I deliberately increased the complexity so the challenge matched the intended recipient better. That meant creating a longer progression while still ensuring that each step gave enough feedback to encourage continued solving. The exterior also had to read clearly as a piano rather than a generic box. That made the internal packaging challenge more interesting, since the mechanism sequence had to fit within the low, wide body and still preserve the overall silhouette.

overview.label: Shared Packaging and reward system
overview.text: Like the other puzzles in the series, The Keys includes the same reward concept and modular display system. The packaging also keeps the same overall dimensions so the products feel related, even though the external identity changes through the logo and the puzzle form itself. Using the same packaging and reward structure helped me focus this design on what changed: the puzzle body, the solving sequence, and the intended difficulty. It also made the series feel more like a coherent line of products rather than unrelated one-off puzzle boxes.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: The Frets is a guitar-shaped mechanical puzzle box designed for my dad. It uses a nine-step solution sequence and is the third puzzle in the same family as The Mic and The Keys.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I wanted the third puzzle in the series to be the most challenging of the three while still being tailored to its intended recipient. Because my dad’s favorite guitar is a Steve Vai Ibanez JEM, I based the form of the puzzle on that instrument rather than using a generic guitar silhouette.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the guitar-shaped enclosure, nine-step puzzle sequence, internal reward mechanism, and the matching packaging presentation. Like the other puzzles in the series, it uses the same overall packaging dimensions and the same modular reward-and-display system, while the puzzle form, identity, and difficulty are specific to the recipient.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was fitting the most difficult mechanism sequence in the series into a highly recognizable guitar form. The puzzle had to preserve key visual cues of the Ibanez JEM while also making room for a longer and more complex solving path.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project pushed me further in balancing form, mechanism density, and user-specific design. It also reinforced how a product family can stay consistent through shared packaging and reward structure while still giving each individual puzzle its own identity and difficulty.

overview.label: Nine-Step puzzle sequence
overview.text: Like The Keys, The Frets uses a nine-step sequence, but it is the hardest puzzle in the series. I increased the difficulty further for this version so the solving experience would feel more substantial for its intended recipient. Because the outer form was based on a specific guitar, the mechanism sequence had to fit around recognizable body and neck geometry rather than inside a simple box. That made the internal packaging challenge more demanding while also giving the final puzzle a much stronger identity.

overview.label: Shared Reward & Packaging System
overview.text: The reward system is the same as the other puzzles in the series, allowing the final reward to connect into the same modular display-stand system. The packaging also keeps the same outer dimensions so the series feels visually and structurally consistent. That shared structure let me focus this design on what changed: the guitar-based form, the higher difficulty, and the recipient-specific identity. Together, the three puzzles function more like a coordinated product line than isolated one-off designs.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: A small automated greenhouse model built around an Arduino Uno R3. The system monitors temperature and ambient light, automatically controls ventilation and lighting, includes adjustable environmental thresholds, and can switch into a manual control mode using an IR remote.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: The project was created for a school assignment exploring Arduino programming and electronic control. I wanted the greenhouse to behave like an integrated system rather than a collection of independently activated components, with sensors, controls, alarms, and mechanical features responding to one another.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the greenhouse enclosure and electronic layout around the Arduino and its peripherals, including labeled external access to the Arduino's USB and power ports. I integrated a servo-powered vent, temperature and light sensing, adjustable controls, automatic/manual operating modes, indicator LEDs, an alarm system, and IR remote control.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was coordinating several inputs and outputs through one control system. Temperature, light level, operating mode, user-adjusted thresholds, and remote commands all had to influence the correct hardware without conflicting with one another.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project helped me move from programming individual Arduino components to thinking in terms of system logic. A useful automated system needs more than sensors and actuators; it also needs adjustable behavior, user overrides, feedback, and a way to recognize when the expected response does not occur.

overview.label: Environmental Automation
overview.text: The temperature sensor controls a servo-driven 3D-printed roof vent. When the measured temperature rises above the selected threshold, the vent opens to increase airflow; when the greenhouse cools, it closes again. A potentiometer connected to the external adjustment knob changes this upper temperature threshold, allowing the user to control how sensitive the system is. A photoresistor performs a similar role for lighting. When ambient light falls below the programmed threshold, the greenhouse activates its yellow LED lighting and switches it off again when sufficient light returns.

overview.label: Manual Control & User Interface
overview.text: A front-mounted button switches the greenhouse between automatic and manual operation. In manual mode, an IR receiver allows a handheld remote to directly control the individual greenhouse systems rather than relying on sensor inputs. The physical design also incorporates the electronics into the enclosure rather than treating them as separate components. The Arduino's USB and external power connections are exposed through labeled openings on the rear of the greenhouse, while the threshold knob and mode button are positioned on the exterior for easy access.

overview.label: Fault Detection & Alarm System
overview.text: I programmed the greenhouse to check not only environmental conditions, but whether the appropriate system responded to them. If temperature or light exceeds its threshold without the corresponding ventilation or lighting system activating, the greenhouse enters an alarm state. A red LED flashes while the piezo buzzer produces an audible warning, providing both visual and audio feedback that the system is outside its intended operating condition. This added a basic layer of fault detection rather than assuming that issuing a command meant the environmental problem had actually been addressed.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: A custom vertical stand for the Dell Pro Max Mini that securely holds the computer without blocking its rear ports, front indicator light, or airflow. Multiple stands can connect horizontally through a folding dovetail system.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: My dad uses three identical computers in one workstation and wanted a cleaner, more organized way to mount them vertically while keeping the setup modern-looking and easy to access.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: Because the computer had just been released and I could not find usable CAD, I recreated its relevant geometry from digital-caliper measurements. I designed the close-fit cradle, ventilation openings, folding connector mechanism, and custom company branding.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The stand needed to hold the computer firmly without making removal difficult, preserve airflow, maintain access to every port and indicator, and support multiple connected units without crowding the computers or their wiring.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: The project reinforced how many constraints can exist in a simple product. Fit, thermal management, cable access, manufacturing tolerances, appearance, and multi-unit use all affected the same geometry.

overview.label: Folding Dovetail Connection System
overview.text: Each stand has a fixed female dovetail on one side and a rotating arm with a male connector on the other. When deployed, the arm links adjacent stands while creating enough spacing between computers for airflow and rear cable management. When unused, it rotates 180 degrees underneath the stand so it does not increase the footprint or leave a connector protruding from the final unit in a row. The arm is a separate FDM-printed part that snaps directly into the stand without pins or hardware. The only design revision was reducing clearance in this snap connection so the arm stayed securely installed while still rotating freely.

overview.label: Manufacturing & Real-World Use
overview.text: The final design consists of only two ABS components printed on a Bambu X1C: the main stand and connector arm. The main stand fit correctly on its first physical iteration, including the close-fit computer cradle. Three completed stands have been connected together and used continuously for several months. The computers remain stable and easy to remove, all ports remain accessible, airflow has not caused thermal issues, and the connector system has remained secure during daily use.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: A custom adjustable pipe connector designed to stabilize the upper structure of an expo booth. It connects two pipes while allowing the angle between them to be adjusted and then locked in place.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I designed this for my dad’s trade-show booth, where the upper frame needed additional stability. The connector also had to work around the booth’s fabric backdrop, which wraps around the pipes and could be damaged by a conventional set-screw clamp.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed a hinged connector with an adjustable joint that can be locked using a top clamping bolt. I also designed the side clamping system so the screws never contact the pipe directly. Instead, each screw pushes a non-rotating internal pad forward to grip the pipe and fabric together.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was creating a connector that could lock its angle securely while clamping onto the pipes without twisting, bunching, or tearing the backdrop material. A normal screw pressing directly against the pipe would rotate against the fabric as it tightened.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project reinforced how much a mechanism can improve when it is designed around the real conditions in which it will be used. The internal pad added only a small amount of complexity, but solved a problem that a simpler clamp would have created.

overview.label: Fabric-Safe Clamping System
overview.text: The most important feature of the connector is its internal clamping pad. Instead of allowing the side screws to bear directly against the pipe, each screw pushes the pad inward without rotating it. Tightening therefore increases clamping force without dragging a spinning screw tip across the booth fabric. This allowed the connector to grip securely while protecting the backdrop wrapped around the frame.

overview.label: Angle Adjustment & Locking
overview.text: The central joint allows the two pipe sockets to rotate relative to each other so the connector can accommodate different booth-frame angles. Once positioned, the top bolt clamps the joint and locks the selected angle in place. This gave the connector enough flexibility for setup while still allowing it to act as a rigid brace once installed.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: A 3D-printed stand designed to hold an Xbox controller in a clean, stable, display-friendly way. The design focuses on a sleek, contemporary appearance while still functioning as a practical everyday desk accessory.

overview.label: Why I worked on it
overview.text: This began as a school project, but I wanted to treat it like a real consumer product rather than just a simple holder. My goal was to create something that looked polished and intentional, with a form that felt modern and visually appealing while securely supporting the controller.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I designed the base, upright support, and controller cradle as a compact desktop product. The stand was intentionally split into two printable parts so it could be manufactured cleanly on an FDM printer, then assembled with a single hidden screw in the base so the final product reads as one seamless object.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was balancing aesthetics, manufacturability, and function. The stand needed to hold the controller securely without looking bulky, and it also needed to print reliably without excessive support material or awkward assembly hardware disrupting the appearance.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project taught me more about designing for both appearance and manufacturing at the same time. Even a simple product benefits from careful attention to print orientation, part breakdown, assembly method, and the way small choices affect how finished and professional the final object feels.

overview.label: Form, Manufacturing, & Assembly
overview.text: I wanted the stand to feel more like a finished retail product than a basic 3D-printed bracket. To do that, I used a smooth, angled cradle and a broad base with softened geometry to give it a more contemporary look. The product was divided into two parts specifically to improve printability and surface quality. After printing, the two sections are joined with one screw inserted from the base, which keeps the connection hidden and makes the stand appear visually clean from normal viewing angles. The finished stand holds the controller securely while also presenting it nicely, making it both a functional storage piece and a display object.

projects.title: Original LEGO Transformers: Overhaul, Liftor & Cargo

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: A set of three original transforming LEGO characters - Overhaul, Liftor, and Cargo - that I designed at around age eleven. Each model converts between a robot and vehicle mode without requiring the model to be disassembled and rebuilt.

overview.label: Why I made it
overview.text: I had become fascinated by how Transformers could rearrange the same physical parts into two recognizable forms and wanted to figure out how to create that process myself. LEGO gave me a way to experiment with transformation mechanisms before I had access to CAD or 3D printing.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I created all three characters and their transformation schemes from scratch, deciding which vehicle components would become specific robot body parts and arranging hinges and joints so the same bricks could function in both modes. I later recreated and documented the designs digitally in BrickLink Studio.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: LEGO imposed fixed part dimensions, connection points, and joint geometry, so every transformation had to work within a predefined mechanical system. The challenge was fitting two forms into the same collection of bricks while keeping both recognizable and making the transformation physically possible.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: These were some of my earliest attempts at spatial mechanism design. They taught me to think about parts not as having one fixed purpose, but as geometry that could change function depending on its position. That idea eventually became central to the more complex transforming figures I designed later.

overview.label: Three Original Designs
overview.text: The three models gave me repeated opportunities to solve the same fundamental problem in different ways. Instead of copying existing Transformers, I created original characters and vehicle modes, then developed transformations around the shapes and LEGO parts available to me. The models are simple compared with my later transforming-figure work, but they document the point where I first moved from studying transformations to designing my own.

overview.label: Early Transformation Design
overview.text: Working in LEGO meant that nearly every joint, pivot, and structural connection came from existing parts rather than custom geometry. I had to search for arrangements that produced the movement I wanted while still creating stable robot and vehicle forms. Looking back at these models alongside my later CAD-designed Transformers shows how the same interest developed as my tools changed: the underlying problem—making one physical object convincingly become another—stayed the same.

overview.label: BrickLink Page
overview.text: Here is the link to my LEGO BrickLink page which contains each of these models with descriptions and additional images as well as transformation sequences: https://www.bricklink.com/v3/studio/public_gallery.page?idUser=3040757

overview.label: What it is
overview.text: A wooden truss bridge model I designed and built for a school engineering project when I was eleven. The structure uses repeated triangular bracing along the sides and top to create a rigid bridge frame from lightweight wooden members.

overview.label: Why I worked on it
overview.text: The project was an early opportunity to take a structure from a digital design into a complete physical build. I wanted the bridge to be structurally organized while also looking like a deliberate, finished design rather than simply meeting the assignment requirements.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I developed the bridge geometry in CAD, including the repeated truss structure, cross-bracing, roadway support, and overall proportions. I then translated that design into individual wooden members and assembled the physical bridge from the resulting plan.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was making a three-dimensional structure from many small individual pieces while keeping repeated sections aligned and consistent. Because errors could accumulate across the length of the bridge, the geometry and assembly order had to be planned before construction.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project was one of my earliest experiences moving from CAD to a real manufactured object. It taught me that a design that looks correct digitally still has to account for assembly, alignment, structural connections, and the limitations of the material used to build it.

overview.label: Truss Structure & Assembly
overview.text: The bridge uses repeating triangular trusses along its length, with additional cross-bracing connecting the two sides into a rigid three-dimensional frame. Repetition allowed the structure to use a relatively small set of member geometries while distributing loads through multiple connected paths. I also planned the build as an assembly rather than treating each piece independently. Constructing the repeated sections consistently was important to keeping the finished bridge straight and allowing the two sides and roof structure to align properly.

overview.label: Prototype Development and Major Architecture Pivot
What it is
overview.text: A compact handheld catapult I designed for a school engineering project at age thirteen. Rather than using the conventional tabletop layout used by most of the class, I arranged the launching mechanism into a compact handheld form with an integrated release mechanism.

overview.label: Why I worked on it
overview.text: I wanted to approach the assignment differently and see whether the same basic catapult principle could be packaged into a much smaller, more unusual structure. The project became an early exercise in rearranging a familiar mechanism around a different form factor.

overview.label: What I designed
overview.text: I sketched the design by hand before fabrication, developing the overall body, compact launching arm, payload cradle, and trigger-based retention system. There was no CAD model; much of the final geometry evolved directly during fabrication as I adjusted proportions and fit by eye.

overview.label: Key engineering challenge
overview.text: The main challenge was packaging the moving mechanism into a small structure while keeping the wooden body rigid and the moving components free to operate. Because the original drawing was not heavily dimensioned, fabrication also required constant adjustment as the physical design developed.

overview.label: What I learned
overview.text: This project showed me both the strengths and limitations of designing directly through fabrication. Freehand iteration made it easy to adapt quickly, but it also taught me why controlled dimensions, tolerances, and CAD become increasingly important as mechanisms grow more complex.

overview.label: Hand Fabrication and Mechanism Development
overview.text: The final prototype was built from wooden panels, beams, and dowels that I cut, sanded, joined, and reinforced by hand. I focused on producing a smooth, structurally stable body rather than leaving the project as a rough proof of concept. The mechanism used stored elastic energy and a mechanical release so the moving arm could remain restrained until intentionally triggered. Developing the mechanism directly in wood required repeated fitting and adjustment rather than the dimension-driven workflow I use for later CAD projects.
